Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette: Giancarlo's eyes still flinch when he recalls the warehouse fire that ravaged his hometown five years ago. As a counselor, he had been working with families displaced by the disaster, but nothing could have prepared him for the scent of smoke and burning plastic that still wafts through his mind like a specter. When the aroma of burnt food or smoke from a nearby BBQ drifts into his office, Giancarlo's heart quickens, and he feels an overwhelming urge to escape – to avoid the memories that come flooding back. He has become adept at dodging social invitations, citing work commitments or feigning fatigue. "I'm just not ready to see friends yet," he tells himself, though the truth is more complicated. Giancarlo fears that if he allows himself to relax around others, his thoughts might begin to unravel, and he'll lose control – a prospect that fills him with dread. He has taken to monitoring his own thoughts obsessively, searching for signs of instability or impending madness. The memories themselves are disjointed, as if they belong to someone else. Giancarlo recalls the panic, the screaming, and the desperation, but it's all filtered through a haze of smoke and chaos. When he does think about that day, the emotions come rushing back – the fear, the helplessness – without any clear images or context. He might be walking down the street when suddenly, out of nowhere, his heart is racing, and he's reliving the terror. Giancarlo has begun to see his body as an unreliable ally, prone to reacting as if danger still lurked around every corner. His mind is constantly on high alert, anticipating potential threats – a mindset that leaves him exhausted but vigilant. He has become convinced that thinking about the event will push him over the edge, so he studiously avoids any reminders, no matter how small. The smell of smoke or burning objects can transport Giancarlo back to that terrible day in an instant, and with it comes the crushing weight of memories he'd rather forget. The emotions swell up, unbidden, and he feels like he's drowning all over again. His mind starts racing: "What if I lose control? What if I'm not strong enough?" The memories seem to fuel his hypervigilance, which in turn makes him even more sensitive to triggers – a cycle that has become increasingly hard to break. As the months have passed, Giancarlo's avoidance strategies have taken a toll on his relationships and work. His clients sense his distraction, and his colleagues wonder what's behind his increasing withdrawal. Giancarlo knows he needs help, but the thought of confronting those memories head-on fills him with trepidation. He fears that seeking therapy will mean facing the very demons he's been trying to keep at bay – a prospect that has left him feeling trapped and uncertain about the future. Despite this, something inside Giancarlo has shifted. Perhaps it was the recent anniversary of the fire or the growing realization that his avoidance strategies were no longer sustainable. Whatever the reason, he has finally begun to consider seeking help, though the fear of what might happen if he opens up those old wounds still lingers – a nagging dread that threatens to hold him back from healing once and for all.
